title: Republic of Ireland commits to Israel matches in Nations League due to ‘potential disqualification’
content:
Republic of Ireland will play their Nations League fixtures against Israel due to the threat of “potential disqualification” if they do not.

In November, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) voted to submit a formal motion to UEFA, the governing body of European football, seeking to ban Israel from continental competition.

Its legal arguments claimed two UEFA statutes had been breached by Israel, with the body allegedly failing to implement an effective anti-racism policy, and allowing Israel to organise clubs “in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian FA”.

Republic of Ireland has now been paired with Israel, along with Austria and Kosovo, in Group B3 of the 2026-27 Nations League.

The FAI moved swiftly following Thursday’s draw to clarify its side would play its away game against Israel on September 27 and their home match in Dublin on October 4.

Israel has not hosted UEFA matches since October 2023 due to security issues. All of its ‘home’ matches in 2025 were played at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen, Hungary, while it played ‘home’ games in 2024 in the Hungarian capital of Budapest and the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, Hungary.

A widely circulated FAI statement after Thursday’s read: “In 2025, a motion was proposed by members of the FAI General Assembly to vote on issuing a formal request to the UEFA Executive Committee for the immediate suspension of the Israel Football Association from UEFA competitions for a breach of UEFA statutes.

“Members then voted in favour to submit the motion to UEFA, which the Association did in November 2025.

“While consultation has taken place with UEFA officials, the Association does recognise that UEFA regulations outline that if an association refuses to play a match then that fixture will be forfeited and further disciplinary measures may follow — including potential disqualification from the competition.”

In a statement to The Athletic, an Israel FA spokesperson said: “We are very happy with the draw and are only concerned with its professional aspects. They are challenging enough. The decision on where Ireland will host its games is its own alone. We have no concerns about arriving in Dublin.”

The spokesperson also added they were hopeful that the security situation would improve to allow them to play home matches in Israel “as soon as possible”. UEFA continues to hope for a solution that enables that, sources with knowledge of the governing body’s position, told The Athletic.

In October, Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson said he did not understand why Russian teams was banned from FIFA and UEFA competitions but those from Israel was not.

“I don’t see a difference between FIFA and UEFA banning Russia and not Israel,” said Hallgrimsson, in quotes carried by the Irish Times. “I am not speaking on behalf of the FAI — I just don’t see the difference.”
